pages.text: $(thing)Galena$() is lead sulfide, the lead ore of TFC++. It lies with $(l:the_world/ores_and_minerals#sphalerite)sphalerite$() and barite in limestone, dolomite and marble between y=-30 and 70, and in veins through quartzite, slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss between y=-70 and 40. Prospect it as any ore.$(br2)Lead and silver go together: galena carries 0.3% of silver by the mass of its lead. It was for this silver that Athens mined lead at Laurion.
pages.title: Galena

pages.text: Galena roasts at $(bold)800 °C$() into $(thing)work lead$(), lead with its silver still in it. A piece gives metal by its size: small 10 mB, poor 15, normal 25, rich 35.

The sulfur of galena burns to sulfur dioxide, 1.4 mol from a normal piece, and 3% of its lead goes up as a smoke of lead oxide. Both are poison.$(br2)Roast in the open air or under a flue, and see $(l:tfcpp/sulfides#roasting)Sulfide Ores$() for what sulfur dioxide does in a closed room. The smoke is the slow one, and it is next.
pages.title: What the roast gives off

pages.text: Lead oxide fume does not choke. It collects in the body, with a half-life of 30 days of process time, 12 real hours. Symptoms begin at 30 mg, incapacity at 100 mg, death at 300 mg. Air with 100 mg of fume in each cubic metre adds 1.6 mg a minute to whoever breathes it.$(br2)A full charge in the cupellation hearth makes 370 g of it. See $(l:tfcpp/poisons#chronic)Poisons$().
pages.title: The smoke that kills slowly

pages.text: Silver does not burn and lead does. Hot air over molten lead turns it to $(thing)litharge$() (PbO), which melts at 888 °C and is soaked up by a porous floor of bone ash. The silver stays behind, and when the last film of litharge leaves it, the bright metal flashes: the $(bold)blick$().$(br2)Assayers and mints worked so for thousands of years.
pages.title: Cupellation

pages.text: The $(thing)Cupellation Hearth$() is five fire bricks. It takes the heat of the fire below it, as the coke oven does.
Bone meal heated to 700 °C is $(thing)Bone Ash$(), the floor of the hearth. A powder soaks up the litharge of 500 mB of lead. With no ash the hearth does nothing.

$(li)Lay the floor: right-click with bone ash, a powder for each 500 mB of lead.$(li)Light a fire under it: the hearth must reach 960 °C, to keep litharge liquid.$(li)Pour in work lead from a vessel or a mold, up to 1000 mB.$(li)It burns 1 mB of lead a second while the air above it holds over 12% oxygen. A full charge takes 17 minutes.$(li)Litharge drops as powder above the hearth. An empty hand reads its state.
pages.title: Working the hearth

pages.text: When the last lead has gone the silver flashes, with a chime and a message. Right-click with an empty mold to pour it out. Only whole millibuckets come out, and the fraction stays for the next charge.$(br2)A full charge of 1000 mB gives 212 powders of litharge, 3.24 mB of silver and 370 g of lead fume. An ingot of silver (100 mB) takes 31 charges. Plain lead is refused: its silver is gone already.
pages.title: The silver

pages.text: The fume rises into the room, and only moving air takes it into a pipe. A $(l:tfcpp/pipes#pump)piston pump$() draws in the air of the one cell behind its back and delivers it into the pipe in front. It takes whatever that air holds: smoke, the fumes of arsenic, antimony, zinc, lead and mercury, sulfur dioxide. Coal dust it leaves.$(br2)So set the pump with its back to the cell where the fume comes out, the air over the hearth or the furnace, or beside it. A shaft must turn it.
pages.title: How fumes reach a line

pages.text: A turn of the shaft sweeps 20 litres, a fiftieth of a cell. The pump works slowly, so keep it where the fume is thickest, and fit more than one for a big fire.$(br2)The gas enters the line at room temperature, whatever the heat of the fire. A $(l:tfcpp/sulfides#catching)condensation tower$() in the line takes 5% of the oxide fume a second below 250 °C, and mercury below 100 °C. Sulfur dioxide passes through: end the line in a vent in the open air, away from where anyone works, or the pressure builds and the pump stalls.
pages.title: The line and the tower

pages.text: Litharge goes back to metal in the $(l:tfcpp/sulfides#retort)retort$() at 800 °C with carbon: PbO and C give Pb and carbon dioxide. A powder with 0.125 mol of carbon gives 4.57 mB of lead. A charcoal holds 200 mol, enough for 1600 powders.$(br2)Lead does not boil, so no condenser is needed, and the carbon dioxide goes into the room. Of 1000 mB of work lead you get back about 970 mB of clean lead: 3% went up as smoke.
pages.title: Litharge back to lead

pages.text: Lead is beaten into $(thing)sheet$() cold: it recrystallises at room temperature, so it needs no forge. Work lead makes a sheet of work lead the same way, but that sheet melts back into work lead, and no pipe is made of it.

Lead sheet makes pipes, the $(l:tfcpp/acids#chamber)lead chamber$(), the condensation tower and the lead fittings. Lead is the metal that holds sulfuric acid, under a film of its own sulfate.$(br2)It is soft. Its pipe is rated at 5.9 atm and gives at 150 °C, and the metal melts at 327 °C (see $(l:tfcpp/pipes#walls)Pipes and Pressure$()). A sheet melts back into 100 mB of lead.
pages.title: What lead is for
